tier_reason: Every quoted number is in docs/benchmark.mdx of the PcapPlusPlus website repo, a run by PcapPlusPlus's own maintainers with mfontanini/packet-capture-benchmarks (public code: pcapplusplus/benchmark.cpp, libtins/benchmark.cpp, libpcap/benchmark.cpp, benchmark.sh, Makefile.in, configure.ac); g++ 11.4.0 and the i7-8700 are stated but no flags are, and the build flags of the PcapPlusPlus v24.09 and libtins v4.5 libraries (where the parsing happens) are unknown, so not A. The measurement is first-party, not independent, so C rather than B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 11.4.0 on Ubuntu 22.04 (WSL2); no flags stated on the page. In the suite, Makefile.in compiles pcapplusplus/benchmark.cpp with -g -O2 -std=c++11, and libtins/benchmark.cpp with @LIBTINS_CXXFLAGS@, which configure.ac sets after AC_PROG_CXX to the CXXFLAGS plus -std=c++11 (autoconf's default -g -O2 when CXXFLAGS is unset) but replaces with only -I<path> when --with-libtins-include-path is passed. The build flags of the PcapPlusPlus v24.09 and libtins v4.5 libraries themselves are not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party run: the page is on the PcapPlusPlus website and was produced by its maintainers, although the harness (mfontanini/packet-capture-benchmarks, 35 stars, 5 commits, no README or committed results) was written by libtins' author, who added PcapPlusPlus to it in November 2017; the PcapPlusPlus benchmark.cpp in the suite is copied from the PcapPlusPlus repo (Examples/PcapPlusPlus-benchmark). The win over libtins is small (1.06x, 1.19x and 1.26x, derived from page data) on a single virtualized machine (WSL2 on an i7-8700 Windows 10 host), versions PcapPlusPlus v24.09 and libtins v4.5. Timing is the integer-millisecond average of 3 runs over a 500,000-packet generated pcap (payload 742 bytes), so resolution is about 0.5 percent. The DNS test is not identical work: libtins re-parses the UDP RawPDU into a DNS object and materialises query and answer vectors, while PcapPlusPlus walks its already-parsed DnsLayer. PcapPlusPlus is slower than the libpcap loop in all three tests (about 1.6x, 1.6x and 6.7x, derived from page data), but that loop only counts packets without parsing, so it is not a like-for-like baseline. Library build flags are not stated (the earlier note that the libtins benchmark line has no -O flag is only true when --with-libtins-include-path overrides autoconf's -g -O2 default). Neither baseline is in the event-loops-io baseline list (libuv, libevent, epoll, io_uring); PcapPlusPlus is a packet capture and parsing library, so the category fit is weak. The rendered page (pcapplusplus.github.io) was not opened; numbers were read from its MDX source.

notes: All six times and packets-per-second figures match the MDX constants exactly (500000/0.197 = 2,538,071 etc.). Downgraded B to C because the run is first-party (PcapPlusPlus maintainers) even though the harness is libtins' author's; no independent run including PcapPlusPlus was found (libtins.github.io blocked, one search found nothing). Consider a category override: this is packet parsing, not an event loop, and libtins/libpcap are off the category's baseline list.

tier_reason: Independent third-party shootout (guteksan/REST-CPP-benchmark; author not on the Restinio team, linked from the Pistache README) whose results image images/rest_all.PNG shows every quoted figure; code for all six equivalent services and the client (basic-*/main.cpp, postInLoop.py) is public and the CPU is stated, but the compiler is not, so not A.

corrections.workload: Independent shootout (guteksan/REST-CPP-benchmark, 2020): six equivalent services (POST /test echoes the body prefixed with 'Sending response: ', log4cplus logs each request and reply, optional sleep t) driven by 10 Python producer processes (postInLoop.py, http.client, a new TCP connection per request, printing under a shared lock), each sending N=200 or 1000 requests; service thread pool C=28 or C=4; Local (same machine) or VPN; metric is time from the service's first logged request to its last reply, one run per cell.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Read from images/rest_all.PNG. Local, N=1000, t=0 ms: C=28 Restinio v0.6.2 1.025 s vs Restbed v4.6 1.333 s (1.30x faster, derived from page data) and C++ REST SDK 3.401 s (3.32x, derived from page data); C=4 Restinio 0.85 s vs Restbed 1.789 s (2.10x, derived from page data), C++ REST SDK deadlocked. The README: Restinio 'was over 3 times faster than the worst Cpp-REST-SDK'. Restinio is best in both Local sprint cells, but its margin over Pistache is small (1.059 s and 0.964 s, 1.03x and 1.13x, derived from page data); over Crow it is 1.50x and 1.68x (1.536 s, 1.43 s). Over VPN at t=0 Restinio 1:51.788 vs Restbed 1:55.122 (C=28) and 1:48.743 vs 1:48.880 (C=4). With 200 ms handling time all frameworks that complete are within about 3 percent of each other, except Httplib over VPN and Pistache over VPN at C=4 (C++ REST SDK deadlocks at C=4).
corrections.caveats: Independent but obscure (130 stars, 17 commits, 2020) single-run shootout; results exist only as a screenshot (images/rest_all.PNG), times in min:sec.ms with no error bars. The compiler is not stated; services use cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, Restinio v0.6.2 comes from Conan, Restbed v4.6 is a system install with unstated build flags. The client is a Python script that opens a new TCP connection for every request and prints each request and response under a lock, so the client sets a floor and the sprint cells (about 1 s for 10,000 requests) mostly measure connection accept and request handling overhead. Versions are 2020-era (Restinio is now 0.7.10) on a 2016 Xeon E5-2660 v4 under Ubuntu 16.04. The win shows only in the no-delay Local cells; with 200 ms handling time Restinio ties the field (for example 3:21.367 vs Restbed 3:27.542 at C=28, 1:40.859 vs Restbed 1:40.530 over VPN at C=4), and over a VPN the t=0 cells are dominated by network overhead. Restbed is AGPL/commercial; the margin over Pistache is only 3 percent at C=28 and 13 percent at C=4. Restinio's own README makes no measured speed claim and does not cite this benchmark. Neither Restbed nor C++ REST SDK is in the category baseline list (nginx, Go net/http, Boost.Beast, actix-web, uvloop). A Jami issue (git.jami.net, blocked) reportedly measured Restinio at 18,834 req/s vs Restbed 12,677 req/s with ab (10,000 requests, concurrency 20); search snippet only, not opened.

notes: All quoted times match the results image (Restinio 1.025/0.85, Restbed 1.333/1.789, C++ REST SDK 3.401, Pistache 1.059/0.964, Crow 1.536/1.43). Corrected the record's caveat that the margin over Crow is 3 to 12 percent (it is 1.50x and 1.68x; only Pistache is close). Kept B as an independent measurement with public, equivalent service code; same benchmark the cpp-httplib entry uses (there tier C because cpp-httplib did not win).

tier_reason: Upgraded C to B on stronger evidence: the independent guteksan/REST-CPP-benchmark shootout, which the Pistache README itself links, shows Pistache beating C++ REST SDK and Restbed in the Local no-delay cells with equivalent public service code (basic-*/main.cpp, postInLoop.py) and the CPU stated, but no compiler, so not A. The record's 2017 source (binaryspaceship/cpp-rest-frameworks-benchmark) has the numbers as quoted but its harness handicaps both baselines.

corrections.baseline: C++ REST SDK (cpprestsdk) v2.10.15, also Restbed v4.6
corrections.workload: Independent shootout (guteksan/REST-CPP-benchmark, 2020): six equivalent services (POST /test echoes the body, log4cplus logs each request and reply, optional sleep t) driven by 10 Python producer processes (postInLoop.py, http.client, a new TCP connection per request), each sending N=200 or 1000 requests; service thread pool C=28 or C=4; Local or VPN; metric is time from the service's first logged request to its last reply, one run per cell.
corrections.claimed_speedup: From guteksan/REST-CPP-benchmark images/rest_all.PNG. Local, N=1000, t=0 ms: C=28 Pistache v0.0.002 1.059 s vs C++ REST SDK 3.401 s (3.21x faster, derived from page data) and Restbed 1.333 s (1.26x, derived from page data); C=4 Pistache 0.964 s vs Restbed 1.789 s (1.86x, derived from page data), C++ REST SDK deadlocked. Restinio (1.025 s, 0.85 s) is faster than Pistache in both cells. With 200 ms handling time Pistache ties at C=28 but is the slowest or second slowest at C=4 (Local N=1000 8:34.710 vs Restbed 8:21.744; VPN N=1000 10:19.625 vs Restbed 8:23.877). Secondary 2017 source (binaryspaceship/cpp-rest-frameworks-benchmark, ab -n 1000 -c 1 -k, 608,891-byte JSON response): Pistache 319.99 req/s vs Restbed 224.18, cpprestsdk with RapidJSON 47.06 and cpprestsdk default JSON 30.70 (1.43x, 6.8x and 10.4x, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated; services built with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, Pistache linked as a separately built static library (flags not stated). In the 2017 source, bootstrap.sh builds RapidJSON, Pistache, Restbed and every sample with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release in an Ubuntu 16.04 Vagrant box and installs cpprestsdk from the libcpprest-dev package; compiler version not stated.
corrections.hardware: 28x Intel Xeon CPU E5-2660 v4 @ 2.0 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04.3 LTS (guteksan benchmark); the 2017 source states no host CPU (Vagrant VM, CPU count unset in the Vagrantfile).
corrections.caveats: Evidence is dated and modest. guteksan/REST-CPP-benchmark (130 stars, 2020, single run per cell, results only as a screenshot) uses Pistache v0.0.002 against C++ REST SDK v2.10.15 and Restbed v4.6; the Python client opens a new connection per request and prints every reply, so the sprint cells mostly measure connection and request-handling overhead. Pistache wins only the no-delay Local cells (where Restinio is faster still) and trails at C=4 when handlers block for 200 ms; the shootout's README says Restbed (at C=28) and Pistache (with limited threads) 'slightly fall behind' when requests need processing. The 2017 binaryspaceship benchmark (23 stars, commits 2017-06-18 to 2017-06-20, Pistache then at oktal/pistache) handicaps both baselines: the Restbed sample sets a default 'Connection: close' header and closes the session, so ab reports Keep-Alive requests: 0 for it, and the cpprestsdk sample ends main() with a busy-spinning while (true); loop in a VM whose CPU count is not set; the cpprestsdk-rapidjson run also shows Keep-Alive requests: 0 and a bimodal latency (median 4 ms, 66th percentile 40 ms). That source is one sequential connection, one run, read from ab screenshots, with no host CPU stated. The Pistache README makes no quantitative speed claim (the GitHub About line says 'high-performance'). Neither baseline is in the category list (nginx, Go net/http, Boost.Beast, actix-web, uvloop).

notes: Both sources' numbers match their images exactly. Switched benchmark_url to the guteksan shootout (linked from the Pistache README, equivalent service code) and raised the tier to B, consistent with the RESTinio entry from the same shootout; the 2017 benchmark stays as secondary evidence with its baseline handicaps (Restbed forced Connection: close, cpprestsdk busy-spin main loop) recorded. baseline_in_list corrected to false (cpprestsdk is not a listed baseline).
